claim: Any editor can create a Wikipedia category by adding it to a page. Deleting, merging, renaming or splitting one goes through Categories for discussion, which stays open at least 7 days. Speedy renames under six narrow criteria wait 48 hours. When I looked, 174 speedy requests were open.
label: read-in-source

claim: Wikipedia's guideline treats categories, lists and navigation templates as complementary, not duplicates. Lists can be annotated, sourced and sectioned. Categories update automatically but cannot carry notes or sources.
label: read-in-source

claim: Studies treat Wikipedia's category structure as a graph with several parents per node and some cycles, not a tree. Researchers usually prune it to a spanning tree before use. The cycle counts I saw are search snippets only.
label: summary-only

claim: A 2017 Meta-Wiki page lists known problems with MediaWiki categories: subcategory-tree upkeep, over- and under-categorisation, bias from uneven subcategories, a single language, inconsistent hierarchies across languages, and unclear category-versus-list choice. It gives no numbers.
label: read-in-source

claim: In September 2014 Stack Overflow had 38,205 tags on 7,990,787 questions. 25.74% of tags were used fewer than 10 times and only 10.40% more than 500 times. There were 2,765 human-made synonym pairs. Creating a tag needed 1,500 reputation and each question takes one to five tags. Quote: "25,74% of the tags are used less than 10 times"
label: measured

claim: Stack Overflow raised the reputation needed to create a tag from 250 to 500 to 1,500. It automatically culled single-use tags older than six months, which its co-founder called 'just a band-aid'. Synonyms remap a variant tag to the main one and are proposed and voted on by users, while merges were moderator-only.
label: read-in-source

claim: A 2015 preprint says that in 2014 users with 2,500 or more reputation could suggest a tag synonym, approved at a vote score of 5 or more and dropped at -2 or less. I could not check the current figure on Stack Overflow's own help pages, which blocked the fetch.
label: read-in-source

claim: GitHub lets repository admins add up to 20 free-form topics per repository, each lowercase letters, numbers and hyphens, 50 characters or less. A separate curated set of 'featured' topics is maintained by pull request in github/explore, whose topic files carry an aliases field. Quote: "Add no more than 20 topics."
label: read-in-source

claim: A 2020 study found over 118K unique user-defined GitHub topics, with only 5% of public repositories carrying any topic (February 2020). GitHub then had 355 featured topics with 777 aliases. I read 777 off a garbled rendering where the digits were doubled, and a search snippet gives the same figure. Quote: "We discovered over 118K unique user-defined topics in our data."
label: measured

claim: The Hugging Face Hub mixes fixed and free metadata. pipeline_tag (task) is validated, license comes from a dropdown with an 'other' escape that needs a name and link, and languages and datasets must be existing identifiers. 'tags' is free, though some tag values have reserved meanings (modality, library, rl-environment). Quote: "you can add any tag you want"
label: read-in-source

claim: npm's package.json docs describe keywords only as an array of strings that helps discovery in npm search, with no stated limit or vocabulary.
label: read-in-source

claim: Awesome-list rules require a Contents section first, with at most one level of nesting and preferably none. New entries go at the bottom of their category. The list must be a non-generated Markdown file and must hold only the best items, not unmaintained or archived ones. Quote: "Awesome lists are curations of the best, not everything."
label: read-in-source

claim: awesome-selfhosted, one of the largest awesome lists (340k stars), keeps one YAML file per entry in a separate data repository and generates its README and website from it. Its README's contents list 95 categories and runs to about 331,000 characters. Quote: "This repository holds data used to generate https://awesome-selfhosted.net"
label: read-in-source

claim: awesome-selfhosted-data defines each tag in its own file with a name and description, plus optional related_tags, external_links and redirect. A tag needs at least 3 projects using it, an entry appears only under the first tag in its list, and software inactive for 6 to 12 months may be removed by automated checks. Quote: "Any tag must have a minimum of 3 software projects referencing it."
label: read-in-source

claim: The best-of-generator tool builds curated lists from a projects.yaml in which every category must be declared with a title. It marks projects inactive after 6 months and dead after 12 by default. It warns that GitHub renders only the first 512 KB of a README and suggests splitting lists of more than 800 projects. Quote: "only renders the first 512 kb of the main README.md file"
label: read-in-source

claim: Our World in Data showed 126 topic pages in 10 areas, 14,037 charts, 38 data explorers and 508 articles on 2026-11-24. Some topics sit under more than one area, and its About page says more than 120 topics and over 14,000 charts.
label: read-in-source

claim: MeSH sorts descriptors into 16 categories and trees up to 13 levels deep. A descriptor can sit in several tree locations with no primary one, and its tree numbers can change between revisions.
label: read-in-source

claim: MeSH is released once a year, in late November. New terms are suggested through a help-desk form with citations and judged on 'literary warrant', meaning use in the literature. The 2026 release added 160 new descriptors and changed 42. Quote: "Of the 160 new 2026 MeSH descriptors, only 21 were added to the NLM Classification index."
label: read-in-source

claim: Ranganathan's faceted scheme builds classes from five facets (Personality, Matter, Energy, Space, Time), and faceted schemes place new subjects more easily than enumerative trees. Critics note they take more effort to set up and handle marginal new topics less readily. One cited source says online searches usually use no more than three or four facets. Quote: "usually there are no more than three or four"
label: read-in-source

claim: Nielsen Norman Group's 2018 guidance on filters sets no maximum number of facets or values. It asks for mutually exclusive categories, no jargon, general filters first, and labels and values drawn from user research. Quote: "Filters are useless if people don't understand what they mean."
label: read-in-source

claim: In two studies of personal files and email (75 Gmail users; 23 Windows 7 users over 7 weeks), people strongly preferred folders to tags for storing and finding items. They usually gave one tag per item and rarely used multiple tags to find things. Tags gave lower retrieval success and slower retrieval.
label: measured

claim: A Drexel dissertation found folders-only and tags-only setups about equal on organising time, re-finding time and correctness, with tags needing the fewest clicks. I saw only a search summary.
label: summary-only

claim: A 2005 study of collaborative tagging found the relative proportions of tags on a given URL settle into a stable pattern over time, which suggests free tags converge per item rather than sprawling without limit. Quote: "a remarkable stability in the relative proportions of tags within a given url"
label: read-in-source

claim: A 2007 paper argues the line between free tagging and controlled vocabularies is less strict than claimed, since feedback such as seeing others' tags pushes users toward consensus. Synonyms and homonyms remain the main problems a controlled vocabulary solves.
label: read-in-source

claim: A search summary reports that normalising word forms cut a del.icio.us tag vocabulary by about 60%, and that only about 50% of user tags could be mapped to a general controlled vocabulary. I did not open the papers.
label: summary-only

claim: The post that started architecture decision records (2011-11-15) numbers records in one running sequence and says numbers are never reused. Quote: "ADRs will be numbered sequentially and monotonically."
label: read-in-source

claim: The same 2011 post keeps a reversed decision in the repository and marks it as superseded, with a reference to its replacement. Quote: "we will keep the old one around, but mark it as superseded"
label: read-in-source

claim: The 2011 post lists four status values: proposed, accepted, deprecated, superseded.
label: read-in-source

claim: The adr-tools command for a superseding record changes both records: the new one is flagged as superseding, and the old one's status is changed to point at the new one. Quote: "changes the status of ADR 9 to indicate that it is superceded by the new ADR"
label: read-in-source

claim: MADR (latest release listed: 4.0.0, 2024-09-17) names files NNNN-title-with-dashes.md with a consecutive number and assumes fewer than 9,999 records per repository. With category subfolders, numbers are unique only inside a category. Quote: "numbers of ADRs are no longer unique throughout the repository, but locally within a category only"
label: read-in-source

claim: The MADR template's optional status field lists: proposed, rejected, accepted, deprecated, and superseded by a named record.
label: read-in-source

claim: An issue in the MADR repository, open since 2020-10-12 and still open on 2026-11-24, reports that two pull requests each created record number 6 and both merged, leaving two records with one number. Quote: "two ADRs with different names but the same number"
label: anecdote

claim: In that MADR issue, commenters object to a date prefix (YYYYMMDD-title) because it is still not unique for two records made the same day and because it is unclear which date to use. The maintainer prefers numbers because they are easy to cite.
label: anecdote

claim: The MADR issue did not end with a new ID scheme. In August 2026 the maintainers kept running numbers and added a check to their lint tool that fails a pull request when two records share a number.
label: read-in-source

claim: Thunderbird's ADR process takes the next free four-digit number; when two patches claim one number, the first committed keeps it and later ones are renumbered. Quote: "subsequently accepted ADR numbers will be incremented accordingly"
label: read-in-source

claim: Cloud Posse's ADR guide uses running index numbers and warns that they can collide when many people contribute at once. Quote: "when many people are contributing ADRs at the same time, the indexes might end up conflicting"
label: read-in-source

claim: The log4brains tool dropped running numbers on 2020-10-16 after a git merge conflict between two branches. A record's ID is now its file name without the extension, in the form YYYYMMDD-title, with the date being the file's creation date. Quote: "An ADR will be uniquely identified by its slug"
label: read-in-source

claim: log4brains sorts records by a date field, then by git creation date, and its own decision record notes that the git creation date does not follow renames. Quote: "does not follow renames"
label: read-in-source

claim: The log4brains README states that an accepted record is immutable and only its status can change; it can be deprecated or superseded by another. Quote: "an ADR is immutable. Only its status can change."
label: read-in-source

claim: AWS's ADR guidance says an accepted (or rejected) record is immutable; a changed decision needs a new record with its own review, and the old record's state is then set to Superseded. Quote: "When the team accepts an ADR, it becomes immutable."
label: read-in-source

claim: Microsoft's Well-Architected guidance (ms.date 2026-04-10) calls the decision record an append-only log: accepted records are not edited, and a changed decision is a new record linked to the one it supersedes. Quote: "Don't go back and edit accepted records."
label: read-in-source

claim: A widely read ADR article (page dated 2026-03-24) says an accepted record is never reopened or changed, only superseded with a link, and that files carry a monotonic number plus a descriptive name. Quote: "it should never be reopened or changed - instead it should be superseded"
label: read-in-source

claim: One public ADR site states the two-tier rule directly: a record is immutable once accepted except for simple fixes that do not change the substance. Its record URLs use a date-plus-slug form (YYYYMMDD-slug). Quote: "beyond simple fixes and improvements that don't change the substance of the decision"
label: read-in-source

claim: Thunderbird's ADR process allows editing an existing record over time, not only its status. Quote: "An ADR can be updated over time, either to change the status or to add more information."
label: read-in-source

claim: Rust RFCs start as a file named 0000-my-feature.md. The number is the pull request's number, so it is assigned by the hosting platform when the pull request opens, and the file is then renamed. Quote: "Don't assign an RFC number yet; This is going to be the PR number."
label: read-in-source

claim: The Rust RFCs README gives two different moments for the rename: the author renames after opening the pull request, and elsewhere the team renames the file if the RFC is accepted.
label: read-in-source

claim: Accepted Rust RFCs are not substantially changed. Very minor changes are amendments; larger changes are new RFCs with a note added to the original. Quote: "More substantial changes should be new RFCs, with a note added to the original RFC."
label: read-in-source

claim: Kubernetes enhancement proposals are prefixed with the number of their tracking issue, which the README says gives a unique identifier and a link back to the issue. Quote: "KEPs are now prefixed with their associated tracking issue number."
label: read-in-source

claim: The older KEP process document lets a new proposal be checked in as draft-YYYYMMDD-my-title.md and assigns the number later in a pull request that changes nothing else, to keep merge conflicts small. Quote: "No other changes should be put in that PR so that it can be approved quickly and minimize merge conflicts."
label: read-in-source

claim: KEP status values are provisional, implementable, implemented, deferred, rejected, withdrawn and replaced. The process document pairs 'replaces' on the new proposal with 'superseded-by' on the old one; the current template file shows 'replaces' and 'see-also' but no 'superseded-by' line.
label: read-in-source

claim: The KEP process document says a rejected proposal is kept as a historical document and an implemented one is no longer actively changed.
label: read-in-source

claim: PEP authors pick the next number not used by a published or in-pull-request PEP when naming the file; PEP editors check it or assign one. (PEP 1, last modified 2026-11-08.) Quote: "the next available number (not used by a published or in-PR PEP)"
label: read-in-source

claim: PEP status values are Draft, Active, Accepted, Provisional, Deferred, Rejected, Withdrawn, Final and Superseded.
label: read-in-source

claim: A superseded PEP gets status Superseded and a Superseded-By header; the newer PEP must carry a Replaces header with the old number. PEP 12 says Replaces is only added when the older PEP is in a final state. Quote: "must have a Replaces header containing the number of the PEP that it rendered obsolete"
label: read-in-source

claim: PEPs are not substantially modified after reaching Accepted, Final, Rejected or Superseded. PEP 1 does not spell out a rule for small corrections. Quote: "PEPs are no longer substantially modified after they have reached the Accepted, Final, Rejected or Superseded state."
label: read-in-source

claim: An RFC is never changed after publication (RFC 9280, June 2022, section 7.6), though that document lists this as a historical property that a future policy proposal could affect. Quote: "Once published, RFC Series documents are not changed."
label: read-in-source

claim: RFC errors are handled without touching the RFC: errata are listed separately and are not put into the TXT, PDF or XML files. Statuses are Reported, Verified, Held for Document Update and Rejected; types are Technical and Editorial. (Page last updated 2026-06-11.) Quote: "Errata are not incorporated into the TXT, PDF, or XML formats of RFCs."
label: read-in-source

claim: A new RFC that replaces or amends older ones says so in its own header with Obsoletes and Updates lines (RFC 7322, September 2014, section 4.1.4). That style guide does not define the two words or say how the older RFC is marked.
label: read-in-source

claim: RFC numbers are assigned by one central body, the RFC Production Center (RFC 9280 section 4.3). The RFC Editor FAQ (last updated 2026-11-10) says some numbers were issued and never published, leaving gaps. Quote: "an RFC number is issued prior to publication to a document that does not get published as an RFC"
label: read-in-source

claim: arXiv identifiers since April 2007 are YYMM.number: two-digit year, two-digit month, then a zero-padded sequence number of 4 digits (0704 to 1412) or 5 digits (from 1501). A version is a suffix vN starting at v1; an identifier without a version means the most recent version. Quote: "refers to the most recent version of the article"
label: read-in-source

claim: arXiv removed the subject class from its identifier in 2007 to separate identification from classification, so that a paper can be reclassified after announcement. The old scheme also capped each archive at 999 submissions a month. Quote: "decouple these two properties (identification and classification)"
label: read-in-source

claim: On arXiv every replacement or withdrawal creates a new version number under the same identifier. Every announced version is permanent and cannot be removed. Quote: "may not be removed"
label: read-in-source

claim: An arXiv withdrawal is a new version marked withdrawn. Earlier versions stay accessible with full text, the reason must be given in the public Comments field, and an announced paper cannot be completely removed. Quote: "Articles that have been announced and made public cannot be completely removed."
label: read-in-source

claim: Adding a journal reference or a DOI for the published paper to an arXiv record does not create a new version; the DOI is linked from the abstract page. Quote: "no new article version will be generated when journal reference, DOI or report number information is added"
label: read-in-source

claim: DataCite's relationType list (schema 4.6 and the 'latest' page) has paired relations for versions: IsNewVersionOf and IsPreviousVersionOf, HasVersion and IsVersionOf, Obsoletes and IsObsoletedBy. IsSupersededBy does not appear on either page. Quote: "Indicates A replaces B"
label: read-in-source

claim: DataCite's versioning guide (updated 2026-09-22) keeps the same DOI for minor changes with a raised version number, and recommends a new DOI for major changes; each data steward decides what is major. A 'canonical DOI' for the whole set is recommended only when the versions need to be shown as a group. Quote: "Individual stewards may determine which are major vs. minor versions."
label: read-in-source

claim: DataCite (page updated 2026-08-07) says a DOI cannot be deleted. When the item is removed, the DOI should point to a tombstone page that gives the full citation, the DOI, and a statement that the item is no longer available; a reason is described as helpful. Quote: "a DataCite DOI cannot be deleted"
label: read-in-source

claim: Zenodo registers one DOI per version plus one DOI for all versions, which resolves to the latest version's page. A new version is only for changed files; metadata edits do not create one. Quote: "the landing page of the latest version of your record"
label: read-in-source

claim: Zenodo's General Policies v1.0 say a withdrawn record is replaced by a tombstone page showing the reason, and its DOI and URL are kept. Separately, content judged out of scope can be removed with its DOIs revoked. Quote: "The DOI and the URL of the original object are retained."
label: read-in-source

claim: ICMJE says a retracted article stays public and is clearly labelled as retracted in every form (abstract, full text, PDF). The retraction notice carries the original title in its heading, cites the article, explains why, and is linked with the article in both directions. Quote: "the retraction and original article should be linked in both directions"
label: read-in-source

claim: ICMJE's minimum standard for a correction: publish a correction notice that details the changes and cites the original, post a new article version that says what changed and when, archive all earlier versions, and mark earlier electronic versions as having a newer one. Quote: "Previous electronic versions should prominently note that there are more recent versions of the article."
label: read-in-source

claim: ICMJE describes 'retraction with republication' for an honest error that changes results or conclusions: the changed paper is republished with an explanation. Quote: "retraction with republication of the changed paper, with an explanation"
label: read-in-source

claim: ICMJE treats an expression of concern as a notice an editor may publish while an investigation into alleged misconduct is still running, before any retraction decision.
label: read-in-source

claim: Crossref's versioning guidance (last updated 2025-08-13) says not to modify the original: a correction or retraction is a separate notice with its own DOI that links to the item and states the update type, and the retracted item's title gets a 'RETRACTED:' prefix. Updates are only registered for changes that affect interpretation or crediting. Quote: "You should not modify the original document."
label: read-in-source

claim: Crossmark is a button that shows readers the current status of an item. Crossref's page (last updated 2020-04-08) says there is no extra fee and that members who use it must keep content maintained and register updates promptly. Quote: "There are no additional fees to participate in Crossmark."
label: read-in-source

claim: One large publisher's policy separates retraction (the PDF stays with a watermark and a linked notice) from removal for legal reasons, where the text is replaced by a notice and only the title and authors are kept. Quote: "the metadata (Title and Authors) will be retained"
label: read-in-source

claim: COPE's retraction guidelines could not be opened (HTTP 403 on two routes). Search snippets say they require retracted articles to stay available and be clearly identified as retracted in all electronic sources.
label: summary-only

claim: NISO published a recommended practice on communicating retractions, removals and expressions of concern on 2024-06-27 (RP-45-2024). Only its abstract was read: it covers metadata creation, transfer and display for both the original item and the notice.
label: read-in-source

claim: On GOV.UK a withdrawn page stays at its address with a banner and a public explanation that can link to a replacement; it is hidden from the site's own search. Unpublishing removes the page and needs a redirect, and the guidance says content should not normally be unpublished. Quote: "the page will remain on GOV.UK, but it'll have a banner saying that the content has been withdrawn"
label: read-in-source

claim: GOV.UK allows unpublishing for content published in error or containing personal data, copyright breaches or defamatory material.
label: read-in-source

claim: GOV.UK's guidance says guidance pages should usually be updated in place and not withdrawn. Quote: "should usually be updated rather than withdrawn"
label: read-in-source

claim: GOV.UK's publishing tool shows whether a page is overdue for review, worked out from a review date that an editor set at the last update. The guidance pages read give no fixed review interval. Quote: "based on the review date that someone set when they last updated the content"
label: read-in-source

claim: English Wikipedia's Update tag takes a month-and-year date used for cleanup sorting, and its 'As of' convention files dated statements into categories by month and year so editors can work through the oldest. A sister template, 'Update after', is for a statement that will be out of date at a known future date. Quote: "an alternative for individual statements that will be out-of-date at a specifiable future date"
label: read-in-source

claim: English Wikipedia marks inactive project pages with a notice and keeps them; a separate Superseded tag points to the successor page. Quote: "This page is currently inactive and is retained for historical reference."
label: read-in-source

claim: Microsoft Learn requires an ms.date field on every article, shown to readers as the date of the last substantial edit or freshness check. One Learn article's metadata also carried 'ms.update-cycle: 1095-days'. Quote: "the last time the article was substantially edited or guaranteed fresh"
label: read-in-source

claim: Search snippets from Microsoft documentation repositories say ms.update-cycle defaults to 365 days and is set to other values (180, 1825, 3650 days) per article or per path. No official definition of the field was found.
label: summary-only

claim: MDN's page on banners (last modified 2026-09-02) describes Experimental and Non-standard banners generated from compatibility data and shows only a 'last modified' date. It describes no 'outdated', 'needs review' or 'last reviewed' marker.
label: read-in-source

claim: The NHS digital service manual withdrew its review-date component (page updated November 2021) and replaced it with a pattern showing 'Page last reviewed' and 'Next review due' (page updated November 2025), to be used only when research shows users need it and not when only part of a page was changed. Quote: "We no longer have a review date component."
label: read-in-source

claim: NHS testing in summer 2018 on one health information page found users did not notice review dates placed near the footer under a rule, and read them and found them helpful once moved next to the content. Quote: "users didn't notice them there"
label: anecdote

claim: Ireland's health service manual (updated August 2023) says the team aims to review health content every 3 years and shows last-reviewed and next-review dates at the bottom of the page.
label: read-in-source

claim: A national study of 313 Australian clinical guidelines from 2003 to 2007 found 91 evidence-documented ones; 47 of those 91 (52%) stated a review date, and 14 of the 47 (about 30%) had passed it with no update found. (Published 2010-05-03.) Quote: "a third of these had passed the review date"
label: measured

claim: A survival analysis of 113 recommendations from 4 Spanish national guidelines found 92.0% still valid after 1 year, 85.7% after 2, 81.3% after 3 and 77.8% after 4, and suggests checking every 6 to 12 months. (CMAJ, 2014-11-04.) Quote: "Waiting more than 3 years to review a guideline is potentially too long."
label: measured

claim: A 2016 consensus statement on updating systematic reviews rejects fixed-interval updating. It records that Cochrane moved from updating every two years to updating by need and priority. Quote: "Mechanical rules appear unworkable"
label: read-in-source

claim: The Cochrane Handbook chapter on updating (last updated August 2023) says there is no consensus on when to update and that every review should be assessed periodically to decide whether an update is needed; it sets no interval. Quote: "To date there is no consensus on when to update a review."
label: read-in-source

claim: The Cochrane Handbook cites a study of 100 systematic reviews published 1995 to 2005: median time until an update was needed 5.5 years, 23% out of date within two years, 15% within one year, 7% already at publication. The original study page was blocked.
label: summary-only

claim: Cochrane's living-review chapter (version 6.5.1, 2026) expects searches at least every three months, tells authors to state the last search date and whether new studies were found, and asks for a yearly check on whether the review should stay in living mode. Quote: "at least once every three months"
label: read-in-source

claim: A study of obsolete answers on Stack Overflow reports that 58.4% of them were probably already obsolete when posted and only 20.5% were ever updated after being noted as obsolete. The abstract does not give the sample size. (arXiv, 2019-03-28.) Quote: "only a small proportion (20.5%) of such answers are ever updated"
label: measured

claim: Stack Overflow's Q3 2021 roadmap (2021-07-30) describes an outdated-answers project: a flagging exercise, tests of answer sort order, and a planned Trending sort that weights recent votes more than old ones. The post gives no results. Quote: "weights recent votes more heavily than older votes"
label: read-in-source

claim: Search snippets of Meta Stack Overflow posts say that, as a result of the project, accepted answers are no longer pinned to the top and a Trending sort was added, and quote test success rates of 6.9% pinned against 11.2% unpinned. The posts themselves could not be opened.
label: summary-only

claim: The W3C's 1998 note on stable web addresses says to leave author, subject, status, access level, file extension and software mechanism out of an address, and names the creation date as the one part that will not change. Quote: "Keep the status out of the name"
label: read-in-source

claim: The same W3C note warns against putting a topic in an address because classifications change. Quote: "always look good at the time but change surprisingly fast"
label: read-in-source

claim: The ARK Alliance describes an ARK as resolver, 'ark:' label, a number for the naming organisation, then an assigned name unique within that number. It says creating ARKs costs nothing and that persistence is a matter of management. Quote: "Persistence means persistent management"
label: read-in-source

claim: A PURL is an address that redirects (HTTP 302 by default) to wherever the resource now lives; the maintainer updates the target when it moves. The service is run by the Internet Archive and offers 404 and 410 response types.
label: read-in-source

claim: A 2014 post from a note-taking method site recommends a timestamp ID per note (YYYYMMDDHHMM) because titles and file paths change. Its author hit two notes made in the same minute and added seconds for fast work, and notes that the IDs say nothing about the target. Quote: "Unique identifiers, on the other hand, don't."
label: anecdote

claim: Jekyll requires post files to be named YEAR-MONTH-DAY-title.MARKUP and recommends an internal link tag so links survive a change of address style.
label: read-in-source

claim: Hugo derives a page's address from its file path by default, so a rename changes the address; an 'aliases' list in the page's header creates redirects from the old addresses. Quote: "matches the file path within the `content` directory"
label: read-in-source

claim: Rails names each migration file with a UTC timestamp and a name, and its guide advises against editing a migration already committed: write a new one. Quote: "it contains a UTC timestamp identifying the migration followed by an underscore"
label: read-in-source

claim: In a July 2008 Rails developer thread, a maintainer gave fewer conflicts on branches as the reason for timestamps over running numbers. Objections: the names are ugly, a number is easier to say aloud than a timestamp, and one generator needed a one-second sleep to avoid duplicate timestamps. Quote: "fewer conflicts on branches"
label: anecdote

claim: towncrier keeps one small file per change, named by issue number and type (for example 1234.bugfix), so that contributors do not all edit one file and cause merge conflicts. Files not tied to an issue start with '+'. Quote: "having one single file which developers all write to and produce merge conflicts"
label: read-in-source

claim: OpenStack's reno names each note file with a slug plus a random 16-character hexadecimal suffix. Its design goals are to avoid merge problems and to spare authors from needing any special value; the suffix lets the tool follow a note across edits and renames. Quote: "combines a random suffix with a "slug" value to create the file with a unique name"
label: read-in-source

claim: reno corrects a note by editing its file in place; the note stays tied to the release where it first appeared. Quote: "edit the existing file in place and commit the changes"
label: read-in-source

claim: In the MADR numbering issue, an August 2026 comment separates a noisy merge conflict from a 'silent duplicate' that nothing warns about, and proposes keeping numbers and catching duplicates in CI. The maintainer then added that check to madrlint (2026-08-10). Quote: "silent duplicate"
label: read-in-source

claim: Google's book chapter on documentation describes freshness metadata naming an owner and a review date, with email reminders when a document has not been touched for a set period (example: three months). It says a 'Last reviewed by' byline increased adoption but gives no measurement. Quote: "a low-cost means to ensure that a document is looked over from time to time"
label: read-in-source

claim: The same chapter says that when an internal wiki was retired, around 90% of its documents had had no views or updates in the previous few months. No sample size or method is given. Quote: "around 90% of the documents had no views or updates"
label: read-in-source

claim: English Wikipedia's Disputed tag marks an article whose factual accuracy is contested, expects a talk-page section explaining the dispute, and takes an optional date that a bot fills in if left out. Quote: "This template can take an optional date parameter."
label: read-in-source

claim: DataCite (page updated 2026-08-24) says a DOI cannot be deleted in either Findable or Registered state and its name cannot be changed. A DOI registered in error, or for deleted or retracted content, is moved to Registered (it leaves search but still resolves) and pointed at a tombstone page. Quote: "In both Findable and Registered states, a DOI cannot be deleted."
label: read-in-source

claim: Cloudflare's docs style guide (dateModified 2026-08-20) keeps two dates: Last Updated, taken automatically from git history and refreshed on any content change, and Reviewed, set by hand in front matter when the whole page was read through. Quote: "last explicitly reviewed from beginning to end"
label: read-in-source

claim: Microsoft's hve-core project (page updated 2026-11-06) runs a script that computes each doc's age from its ms.date field: default threshold 90 days, pull request checks fail on stale changed files, and a weekly scan opens one issue per stale file. If the content is still right, the contributor sets the date to today. Quote: "reflects when the content was last meaningfully reviewed or updated"
label: read-in-source

claim: Optimism's curation policy keeps a greppable last-reviewed stamp per page, with a 90-day or 180-day interval by page class. Only a review that re-verified the page may bump it, in the same change; an overdue page counts as a defect and goes first in the next sweep. Quote: "A page past its interval is not automatically wrong, but it is unverified"
label: read-in-source

claim: Search snippets from a documentation vendor's glossary warn that short freshness windows push reviewers to verify without really reading, and that minor edits should not reset the verification date. No study measured this.
label: summary-only

claim: A search snippet said Angular asks reviewers to update a 'Last reviewed' date whether or not they changed anything. The page now served at that address says nothing about review dates, so this could not be confirmed.
label: summary-only

claim: arXiv's copyright help page only says how to report infringement and does not say what happens to a removed paper. Search snippets cite a 2010 report that arXiv moderators removed about 70 papers by 15 authors for plagiarism, and listings marked 'Removed by arXiv admin'.
label: summary-only

claim: A 2024 blog post argues that a readable slug fixes the author's wording into the address at publish time. It describes the id-plus-slug pattern, where only the number is looked up and the slug can change, and for static hosts suggests putting the slug after a question mark. Quote: "This allows the slug to change over time without breaking links"
label: anecdote

claim: Search snippets: a help-centre vendor says links to an article's old address break after a slug change unless a redirect rule is added, and a forum thread argues a slug should never change when a title is edited, since a typo fix can break backlinks.
label: summary-only

claim: Search snippets say the changesets tool names each change file with random human-readable words to avoid collisions and that renaming the file is harmless. Both official routes to the page returned HTTP 404.
label: summary-only

claim: Data Package v2 is the current version of the Frictionless standard. v2.0 was released on 2024-06-26, and the spec pages show a last update of 2026-08-25. The Data Package Working Group accepts changes, and the Open Knowledge Foundation centralises technical maintenance. No v2.1 is mentioned. Quote: "Decision-making on the technical maintenance of the specs will be centralised by OKFN"
label: read-in-source

claim: A Data Resource needs only `name` plus exactly one of `path` or `data`. Every other property is optional, including `hash`, `bytes`, `format`, `mediatype`, `licenses` and `sources`. The v2 JSON Schema enforces this with oneOf of [name, data] or [name, path].
label: read-in-source

claim: `path` may be a fully qualified http(s) or ftp URL or a relative POSIX path. The schema pattern rejects paths that start with `.`, `/` or `~`, or that contain `file:`, backslashes or `/../`. An array of paths may not mix URLs and relative paths. Quote: "A fully qualified URL, or a POSIX file path."
label: read-in-source

claim: In Data Package v2, a bare `hash` value means MD5. Another algorithm is shown by a prefix such as `sha256:<hex>`. The schema pattern is ^([^:]+:[a-fA-F0-9]+|[a-fA-F0-9]{32}|)$, so any prefix is accepted and no list of allowed algorithms is defined. Quote: "The MD5 hash of this resource. Indicate other hashing algorithms with the {algorithm}:{hash} format."
label: read-in-source

claim: The MD5 default was chosen in a GitHub issue that ran from 2013-04-24 to 2013-05-06. The maintainer cited S3 compatibility and acknowledged MD5's vulnerabilities. One search found no current Frictionless proposal to change the default. Quote: "attractive as common (cf s3) but has vulnerabilities"
label: read-in-source

claim: On a Data Resource, `bytes` is an integer size in bytes, `format` is the usual file extension (e.g. csv), `mediatype` is an IANA MIME type, and `encoding` is an IANA preferred name. UTF-8 is recommended for text.
label: read-in-source

claim: `licenses` and `sources` on a resource are inherited from the package when absent. Each licence object needs `name` and/or `path` and may have `title`. The spec defines `name` as an Open Definition licence ID and does not mention SPDX.
label: read-in-source

claim: The Open Definition licence list now has an SPDX ID column. It maps cc-zero to CC0-1.0, odc-pddl to PDDL-1.0, odc-odbl to ODbL-1.0, odc-by to ODC-By-1.0 and cc-by to CC-BY-4.0. The page shows no date.
label: read-in-source

claim: When a Data Package is a directory, its descriptor MUST be named `datapackage.json` at the top level and SHOULD NOT be published under another name. Only `resources` (at least one) is required. `name`, `id`, `licenses` and a profile are SHOULD. Quote: "MUST be named datapackage.json"
label: read-in-source

claim: Package-level `created` must be an RFC 3339 datetime, and `version` SHOULD be SemVer. `contributors` take a `roles` array, with DataCite or CRediT roles suggested. A source object has only title, path, email and version, so there is no field for the date a source was accessed.
label: read-in-source

claim: The standard's own adoption page, updated 2026-08-25, lists 33 entries. Dryad and Our World in Data are listed as data portals, and GitHub, GBIF and the European Commission as community projects. The page gives no detail on how each one uses the standard.
label: vendor-claim

claim: Camtrap DP, a camera-trap data exchange standard, is built as a Frictionless Data Package: a datapackage.json plus three CSV tables, validated with the frictionless tool. This was seen only in search snippets of its site.
label: summary-only

claim: Hugging Face dataset and model cards keep their metadata in a YAML block between `---` lines at the top of README.md. The Hub renders the README as the card. huggingface_hub parses it into CardData and can write it back as YAML. Quote: "Tags are defined in a YAML metadata section at the top of the README.md file."
label: read-in-source

claim: The Hub checks some card fields against fixed lists. `license` must be one of about 80 Hub identifiers, or `other` with `license_name` and `license_link`. `task_categories` points to a fixed pipelines list. `language` must be an ISO 639-1, 639-2 or 639-3 code or a special value. `tags` are free-form.
label: read-in-source

claim: huggingface_hub's RepoCard.validate() sends the card to the Hub's online validation and raises ValueError if it fails. push_to_hub calls it internally. An `ignore_metadata_errors` flag skips metadata parse errors, at the risk of losing information. Quote: "Validates card against Hugging Face Hub's card validation logic."
label: read-in-source

claim: In September 2024, a user's upload with `license: llama3.1` was rejected with a Bad request error. The error said the licence must be one of a fixed list. It was resolved by a docs pull request that added the licence to the Hub's list. Quote: ""license" must be one of [apache-2.0, mit, openrail, ..."
label: anecdote

claim: In July 2022, a model page showed a YAML Metadata Error because the language value "protein" was not an ISO 639 code. A repo with no card metadata shows a warning instead of being blocked. Quote: "YAML Metadata Warning: empty or missing yaml metadata in repo card"
label: anecdote

claim: In July 2022, HF staff opened "Fix `license` metadata" pull requests on many community datasets, to make dataset metadata consistent with models and spaces. In other words, they cleaned up invalid values after the fact. Quote: "We recently updated the datasets metadata for consistency with other repo types (models & spaces)"
label: read-in-source

claim: huggingface_hub documents enumerated options for some dataset-card fields. annotations_creators takes found, crowdsourced, expert-generated, machine-generated, no-annotation or other. multilinguality takes monolingual, multilingual, translation or other. size_categories uses bins such as n<1K and 100K<n<1M.
label: read-in-source

claim: The default dataset card template has these sections: Dataset Details (Description, Sources), Uses (Direct, Out-of-Scope), Dataset Structure, Dataset Creation (Curation Rationale, Source Data, Annotations), Bias, Risks and Limitations, Citation, Glossary, More Information, Dataset Card Authors and Dataset Card Contact.
label: read-in-source

claim: The Hub's licence identifiers are lowercase and not all are SPDX IDs. It uses cc0-1.0, cc-by-4.0 and cdla-permissive-2.0, but has only family IDs `odbl`, `odc-by` and `pddl` where SPDX has ODbL-1.0, ODC-By-1.0 and PDDL-1.0.
label: read-in-source

claim: Google's Dataset structured data requires only `name` and `description`, and the description must be 50 to 5000 characters. Recommended properties include creator, citation, identifier, isAccessibleForFree, keywords, license, sameAs, version, url and hasPart/isPartOf. If `distribution` is given, `distribution.contentUrl` is required and `encodingFormat` is recommended. Quote: "The summary must be between 50 and 5000 characters long."
label: read-in-source

claim: Google's Dataset guide does not mention sha256, dateModified or creativeWorkStatus in its property tables. It mentions isBasedOn only in its guidance on sources.
label: read-in-source

claim: schema.org (V30.1, 2026-09-16) defines `sha256` (Text) on MediaObject, which DataDownload inherits along with contentUrl, contentSize and encodingFormat. So schema.org can also carry a link, a SHA-256 and a size per file.
label: read-in-source

claim: isBasedOn, version, license, dateModified, creativeWorkStatus, correction and isPartOf are CreativeWork properties that Dataset and Article subtypes inherit. `correction` accepts CorrectionComment, Text or URL. Quote: "Indicates a correction to a CreativeWork, either via a CorrectionComment, textually or in another document."
label: read-in-source

claim: schema.org's `supersededBy` is a meta property for vocabulary terms. Its domain and range are Class, Enumeration and Property, so it is not meant for a superseded CreativeWork such as a write-up. Quote: "Relates a term (i.e. a property, class or enumeration) to one that supersedes it."
label: read-in-source

claim: Report, ScholarlyArticle and TechArticle are all subtypes of Article. Report is defined as generated by a governmental or non-governmental organisation, with its own `reportNumber`. TechArticle covers how-to and specification content. Quote: "A Report generated by governmental or non-governmental organization."
label: read-in-source

claim: The current DataCite Metadata Schema is 4.7, released 2026-03-03. It added the resourceTypeGeneral values Poster and Presentation, a relationType `Other`, a `relationTypeInformation` sub-property, and the RAiD and SWHID identifier types.
label: read-in-source

claim: DataCite 4.7 has 6 mandatory properties: Identifier, Creator, Title, Publisher, PublicationYear and ResourceType. It has 6 recommended ones: Subject, Contributor, Date, RelatedIdentifier, Description and GeoLocation. The rest are optional, including Version, Rights, Size and Format.
label: read-in-source

claim: DataCite 4.7 lists 34 resourceTypeGeneral values, including Report, Dataset, Text, Preprint and Collection. Report is defined as a document that presents information in an organised format for a specific audience and purpose. Quote: "A document that presents information in an organized format for a specific audience and purpose."
label: read-in-source

claim: DataCite 4.7 lists 39 relationType values. They include IsSupplementedBy/IsSupplementTo, IsDerivedFrom/IsSourceOf, Cites/IsCitedBy, IsNewVersionOf/IsPreviousVersionOf, HasVersion/IsVersionOf and Obsoletes/IsObsoletedBy. `Other` requires a relationTypeInformation value.
label: read-in-source

claim: DataCite Rights is optional and repeatable (0-n). Its sub-properties are rightsURI, rightsIdentifier (example CC-BY-4.0), rightsIdentifierScheme (example SPDX) and schemeURI (https://spdx.org/licenses/). SPDX is the suggested scheme but is not required.
label: read-in-source

claim: A CITATION.cff in the root of a repository's default branch makes GitHub add a "Cite this repository" sidebar link with APA and BibTeX output. `preferred-citation` redirects the citation to another work, and `type: dataset` gives a data citation. Quote: "We currently support APA and BibTeX file formats."
label: read-in-source

claim: RO-Crate keeps its metadata in one JSON-LD file named ro-crate-metadata.json, using schema.org terms. The root Data Entity is typed Dataset and MUST have name, description, datePublished and license. The spec index calls 1.3 the current long-term release, with no dates shown.
label: read-in-source

claim: CodeMeta is a schema.org-based JSON-LD vocabulary for software metadata, kept in codemeta.json. Its GitHub release list marks 4.0 as latest, but the list shows day and month only (29 Sep) and the README still shows a 3.1 badge.
label: read-in-source

claim: DCMI Metadata Terms (issued 2020-01-20) include provenance, license, source, replaces, isReplacedBy, isVersionOf, conformsTo and modified. `provenance` is a statement of changes in ownership and custody, and `source` is a related resource the described one is derived from. Quote: "A related resource that supplants, displaces, or supersedes the described resource."
label: read-in-source

claim: The FAIR principles (Scientific Data, 2016-03-15) have 15 sub-principles. They include a globally unique, persistent identifier (F1), metadata that stays available even when the data are not (A2), a clear usage licence (R1.1), detailed provenance (R1.2) and domain community standards (R1.3). Quote: "(meta)data are associated with detailed provenance"
label: read-in-source

claim: Datasheets for Datasets (arXiv v1 2018-03-23, published in CACM in December 2021) groups its questions into seven sections. They are motivation, composition, collection process, preprocessing/cleaning/labeling, uses, distribution and maintenance. The authors say datasheet creation is not intended to be automated. Quote: "the process of creating a datasheet is not intended to be automated"
label: read-in-source

claim: W3C PROV models provenance as Entities, Activities and Agents. The relations include used, wasGeneratedBy, wasDerivedFrom, wasAttributedTo, wasAssociatedWith and wasRevisionOf. PROV-DM, PROV-O, PROV-N and PROV-CONSTRAINTS became W3C Recommendations on 2013-04-30, in a 12-document family.
label: read-in-source

claim: On 2013-02-05 the PROV Working Group reported 36 applications using PROV, 12 extensions of PROV-O and 5 datasets. These counts were self-reported. Two searches found no study of PROV use by project size. Quote: "We have reports of 36 applications using PROV, 12 extensions of PROV-O and 5 datasets using PROV."
label: read-in-source

claim: Our World in Data's ETL requires these origin fields: producer, title, date_published, date_accessed, url_main, license.name and citation_full. Indicators require title, unit, short_unit, description_short, processing_level (minor or major) and license. Datasets require update_period_days.
label: read-in-source

claim: OWID keeps code and YAML metadata in git. Each snapshot has a `.dvc` file in git that holds the origin metadata plus the file's md5, size and path. The files themselves go to the Cloudflare R2 buckets owid-snapshots (public) and owid-snapshots-private, and an older version can be pulled by restoring an old md5 and size. Quote: "the public bucket (r2:owid-snapshots/)"
label: read-in-source

claim: A GitHub blog post (2013-09-27, updated 2019-01-04) says GitHub renders YAML front matter at the top of a prose document as a horizontal table. The github/markup README does not mention this, and no current GitHub docs page confirming the behaviour was found. Quote: "this metadata within GitHub as an horizontal table"
label: read-in-source

claim: GitHub's own docs site keeps page metadata in YAML front matter. A schema in its test suite validates every page's front matter. `title` and `versions` are required. Quote: "There's also a schema that's used by the test suite to validate every page's frontmatter."
label: read-in-source

claim: MDN's content repository validates YAML front matter with a Node script, scripts/front-matter_linter.js. The script uses Ajv against a JSON schema in front-matter-config.json and lists ajv, ajv-formats, gray-matter and yaml as devDependencies. A large repo can do it, but with npm packages, not plain Node.
label: read-in-source

claim: Microsoft Learn requires author, description (75-300 characters), ms.author, ms.date and title in each article's YAML front matter. A missing one likely fails validation at build time. Metadata can also be set globally in docfx.json. Quote: "If you omit any of these, you'll likely get a validation error during build."
label: read-in-source

claim: Each GitLab documentation page has YAML front matter with stage, group, info and title. Scripts consume it, for example to build CODEOWNERS, but the page describes no front-matter validation step. Quote: "Each documentation Markdown page contains YAML front matter."
label: read-in-source

claim: The Node.js v26.13.1 module docs list no built-in YAML module. The node:-prefixed built-ins listed are ffi, sea, sqlite, test and test/reporters, while .json files load natively. Two searches found no Node core YAML proposal, only the userland packages js-yaml and yaml.
label: read-in-source

claim: JSON front matter is a supported convention in some tools. Hugo accepts a bare JSON object at the top of a content file. gray-matter parses JSON, YAML and JavaScript front matter by default, with the language named after the opening delimiter (e.g. ---json). Quote: "Hugo determines the front matter format by examining the delimiters that separate the front matter from the page content."
label: read-in-source

claim: The sidematter format (v0.0.4, 2025-08-07) names side files basename.meta.json or basename.meta.yml and prefers JSON when both exist. It suggests front matter for small metadata on text files, and says metadata should usually live in one place. Quote: "If both are present, the convention is to prefer the JSON."
label: read-in-source

claim: Two differently worded searches found no concrete report of side-car metadata files drifting out of sync with the Markdown they describe. Only general docs-as-code drift warnings turned up.
label: summary-only

claim: NIST (2022-12-15) said SHA-1 should be phased out by 2030-12-31, with SHA-2 and SHA-3 as replacements. Quote: "phased out by Dec. 31, 2030"
label: read-in-source

claim: RFC 6151 (March 2011) says MD5 is no longer acceptable where collision resistance is required. It also says an MD5 checksum used only to detect errors is still acceptable. Quote: "MD5 is no longer acceptable where collision resistance is required such as digital signatures"
label: read-in-source

claim: SPDX License List 3.29.0 (2026-09-16) includes CC0-1.0, CC-BY-4.0, CC-BY-SA-4.0, CDLA-Permissive-2.0, ODbL-1.0, PDDL-1.0 and ODC-By-1.0 as exact identifiers.
label: read-in-source

claim: The nixpkgs RFC that created pkgs/by-name says the shared registration file all-packages.nix frequently causes merge conflicts for every new package; packages in pkgs/by-name are picked up automatically without editing that file. Quote: "frequently causes merge conflicts. It's a point of contention for all new packages"
label: read-in-source

claim: nixpkgs shards pkgs/by-name by the lowercased first two letters of the package name. The RFC measured 17,305 top-level names spread over 726 shards, the largest (li) holding 1,092, and calls 1,000 entries GitHub's directory display limit.
label: measured

claim: The nixpkgs contributing guide says its high change rate makes any pull request that stays open too long subject to merge conflicts, so timely review is key. Quote: "The high change rate makes any PR that remains open for too long subject to merge conflicts."
label: read-in-source

claim: GitLab's 2018 post says a single shared CHANGELOG caused constant merge conflicts between merge requests; placeholder lines lessened but did not solve it. The fix was one YAML file per entry in an unreleased folder, compiled into the changelog by release tooling. The post gives no counts. Quote: "The problem was lessened, but not solved."
label: read-in-source

claim: GitLab's current docs generate each CHANGELOG.md entry from the subject line of a commit that carries a Changelog trailer, so contributors do not edit the changelog file.
label: read-in-source

claim: towncrier (docs version 26.9.0) describes itself as the alternative to one single file that all developers write to and that produces merge conflicts; it reads per-change news fragments instead. Quote: "having one single file which developers all write to and produce merge conflicts"
label: read-in-source

claim: reno's design constraints include avoiding merge issues when many release-note-worthy changes land, and keeping notes in git history so they are tagged with the release. Quote: "We want to avoid merge issues when shepherding in a lot of release-note-worthy changes."
label: read-in-source

claim: The Changesets README on main is the development branch for v3 and states what the tool does but no reason about merge conflicts; two guessed docs pages returned 404 and the landing page and CLI README gave no design reasons.
label: read-in-source

claim: tldr-pages runs lint, tests and a build on every pull request, but builds the PDF and runs its deploy step (with a DEPLOY_KEY secret) only on pushes to main, after merge.
label: read-in-source

claim: tldr's maintainer guide warns that merging several pull requests at once can make the post-merge deploy fail, and says to re-run only the workflow of the last merged commit so older runs do not overwrite assets.
label: read-in-source

claim: awesome-selfhosted-data keeps one YAML file per entry under software/. Its pull_request workflow only lints and renders the Markdown; on push to master a separate workflow renders Markdown and HTML and pushes them with deploy keys to two other repositories.
label: read-in-source

claim: DefinitelyTyped tells contributors never to edit .github/CODEOWNERS; owners are listed in each package's package.json and synced to CODEOWNERS once a week. Quote: "do not modify `.github/CODEOWNERS`, always modify list of the owners in `package.json`"
label: read-in-source

claim: DefinitelyTyped does not require correct formatting to merge: unformatted code is reformatted automatically after merge. Quote: "Any unformatted code will be automatically reformatted after being merged."
label: read-in-source

claim: Homebrew tells maintainers to leave the bottle block to BrewTestBot, which builds bottles in CI and performs an automatic merge with bottles after approval for most formula pull requests. Quote: "Please keep bottle block in place; @BrewTestBot takes care of it."
label: read-in-source

claim: cdnjs splits a human repository of JSON package files from a robot-only repository of assets; after merge an auto-updater running roughly hourly fills in the 10 most recent versions.
label: read-in-source

claim: A GitHub Community discussion asking for merge=union support in pull requests has been open since 2021-12-24, is marked unanswered with no staff reply, and users report pull requests ignoring .gitattributes as recently as 2026-10-02. A 2017 support reply quoted there is secondhand.
label: anecdote

claim: No docs.github.com page stating whether pull request merges honour merge=union was found in this session's search.
label: read-in-source

claim: Git's manual says the union driver keeps lines from both sides, tends to leave added lines in random order, and should not be used without understanding the implications. Quote: "This tends to leave the added lines in the resulting file in random order"
label: read-in-source

claim: GitLab says custom merge drivers are not supported on GitLab.com or GitLab Dedicated, and that a merge driver runs only on non-trivial conflicts, so it is not a reliable way to prevent merges. Quote: "so it is not a reliable way of preventing some files from being merged"
label: read-in-source

claim: pnpm says to commit pnpm-lock.yaml and that it can resolve lockfile merge conflicts itself: run pnpm install and commit. This is a generated file kept in each pull request, made cheap to fix by the tool. Quote: "pnpm can automatically resolve merge conflicts in `pnpm-lock.yaml`."
label: read-in-source

claim: GitHub's strict required status checks, the default, require a branch to be up to date with the base before merge; GitHub notes this means more builds as other pull requests merge. Quote: "This is the default behavior for required status checks."
label: read-in-source

claim: Marking a path linguist-generated in .gitattributes hides it in pull request diffs by default; the page says nothing about merging.
label: read-in-source

claim: A search for a merge queue that regenerates a shared generated file on each pull request found no primary source describing that as standard practice.
label: read-in-source

claim: On the pull_request event from a fork, secrets other than GITHUB_TOKEN are not passed to the runner and GITHUB_TOKEN is read-only. Dependabot pull requests are treated the same way. Quote: "The `GITHUB_TOKEN` has read-only permissions in pull requests from forked repositories."
label: read-in-source

claim: pull_request_target runs in the context of the base repository's default branch with secrets; GitHub says to avoid it if you need to build or run code from the pull request. Quote: "Avoid using this event if you need to build or run code from the pull request."
label: read-in-source

claim: A workflow started by workflow_run can access secrets and write tokens even if the workflow that triggered it could not.
label: read-in-source

claim: Secrets cannot be referenced directly in if: conditionals. GitHub's documented way is to set the secret as a job-level environment variable and test that variable; an unset secret evaluates to an empty string. Quote: "Secrets cannot be directly referenced in `if:` conditionals."
label: read-in-source

claim: Public repositories have three approval settings for fork workflow runs (first-time contributors new to GitHub, first-time contributors, all external contributors); by default all first-time contributors need approval. GitHub warns one merged typo fix removes the first-time requirement. Quote: "By default, all first-time contributors require approval to run workflows."
label: read-in-source

claim: Workflows triggered by pull_request_target always run regardless of the fork approval settings. Quote: "will always run, regardless of approval settings"
label: read-in-source

claim: Fork workflow runs awaiting approval for more than 30 days expire and are marked failed; only people with write access can approve them.
label: read-in-source

claim: GitHub's page on pull_request_target says it will enforce, on 2026-12-02, a default policy that blocks pull_request_target in public repositories without an Actions event policy; it is in evaluate mode now. Quote: "On December 2, 2026, GitHub will enforce the default policy"
label: read-in-source

claim: GitHub Security Lab calls a 'safe to test' label gate a temporary solution because of a race with later commits, and says artifacts from untrusted pull requests are themselves untrusted. Quote: "Artifacts resulting from untrusted PR data are themselves untrusted"
label: read-in-source

claim: For a new repository in a personal account, GITHUB_TOKEN by default has only read access to contents and packages.
label: read-in-source

claim: claude-code-action's allow_fork_prs input defaults to 'false': it skips fork pull requests before checking anything out, and the step still succeeds, so a required check that only runs the action passes without a review. Quote: "a required check that only runs the action passes without a review"
label: read-in-source

claim: claude-code-action runs only for actors with write access unless allowed_non_write_users is set; that input requires github_token, bypasses the check, and the action warns its secret scrub reduces but does not eliminate prompt injection risk. Quote: "This reduces but does not eliminate prompt injection risk"
label: read-in-source

claim: claude-code-action's restrict_untrusted_prs defaults to 'true' and denies package managers, test runners, interpreters and shells on pull requests whose author lacks write access, even if claude_args allows them.
